batch_name: Sericon, Vegetable Stone, Practical Exegesis, and Decknamen
description: Concept entries for key terms in the sericonian tradition of English alchemy: the vegetable stone (medicinal elixir), practical exegesis (Rampling's analytical concept), and Decknamen (scholarly term for alchemical cover names). Primary source: Jennifer M. Rampling, 'Transmuting Sericon: Alchemy as Practical Exegesis in Early Modern England,' Osiris 29:1 (2014) pp.19-34.

concepts.label: Vegetable Stone
concepts.definition_long:
The vegetable stone (lapis vegetabilis) is a category of alchemical elixir, distinct from the transmutational mineral stone and the animal stone, that predominates in the English pseudo-Lullian alchemical tradition from the fifteenth century through the seventeenth century. Jennifer M. Rampling, in Osiris (2014), identifies the vegetable stone as a medicinal elixir that 'does not contain toxic corrosives' and was thought capable of curing sickness and prolonging human life; unlike the mineral stone, which aimed at the transmutation of base metals into gold, the vegetable stone operated through 'vegetable' solvents — principally distilled wine, vinegar, and tartar — rather than mineral acids. The three-stone framework (mineral, vegetable, animal) derives from the pseudo-Aristotelian Secretum secretorum and recurs in the pseudo-Lullian Epistola accurtationis; it formed the structural framework of George Ripley's Medulla alchimiae (1476), in which three separate chapters describe the preparation of each stone from its respective starting materials.

In Ripley's system, the vegetable stone was made from 'sericon' — a Deckname for calcined red lead (minium) — dissolved in distilled wine vinegar to form lead acetate, which was then distilled to yield an extremely volatile 'stinking menstruum' (menstruum foetens). Rampling traces how the identity of sericon — and thus the practical basis of the vegetable stone — was repeatedly reinterpreted by successive generations of English alchemists: Elizabethan practitioners including Clement Draper and Thomas Potter substituted copper and other metallic bodies; from the mid-sixteenth century, antimony increasingly displaced lead as the preferred prime matter for sericonian vegetable stone recipes, a transformation driven by the Paracelsian pharmacological interest in antimony preparations; and by the seventeenth century, George Starkey (writing as Eirenaeus Philalethes) developed an explicitly antimonial approach that eclipsed the original lead-based method. This trajectory exemplifies Rampling's concept of 'practical exegesis': the feedback loop by which practitioners maintained the authority of past adepts while adapting their actual practice to new materials. The term 'vegetable stone' continued in circulation in English alchemical writing well into the seventeenth century; it appears in the works of Samuel Norton (d. 1604), Elias Ashmole (1617–1692), and the printed Ripley corpus published by Ludwig Combach in 1649.

concepts.label: Practical Exegesis
concepts.definition_long:
Practical exegesis is a historiographical concept introduced by Jennifer M. Rampling in her study 'Transmuting Sericon: Alchemy as Practical Exegesis in Early Modern England' (Osiris 29:1, 2014) to describe the 'feedback loop' by which early modern alchemical practitioners reinterpreted the inherited textual tradition in light of their own experimental findings, then fed those findings back into the authoritative texts through glossing, annotation, transcription, and copying. Rampling defines it as 'a kind of practical exegesis, in which specific processes and products have been reinterpreted to accommodate such considerations as availability of materials and compatibility with the practitioner's own empirical observations.' The resulting process was not merely passive transmission but active reinterpretation: practitioners modified recipes to fit practical findings, reframed practices to fit established tropes, and reidentified cover names (Decknamen) to match new materials — all while maintaining the outward appearance of fidelity to their predecessors.

The paradigm case Rampling traces is the history of sericon, a Deckname (cover name) in the English pseudo-Lullian tradition: originally denoting calcined red lead in George Ripley's Medulla alchimiae (1476), sericon was progressively reinterpreted as copper, antimony, and other metallic bodies by successive generations of readers, each of whom found the authoritative language compatible with their own preferred materials. The retention of authoritative language — the same Decknamen, the same textual citations — served to mask these practical interventions, making practical exegesis an invisible yet historically significant driver of change in alchemical practice over two centuries. Rampling situates this concept within the broader problem of reading alchemical texts across time: since many texts were printed long after their 'life cycle' began, modern readings may unwittingly be shaped by sixteenth- or seventeenth-century glossators who had already reinterpreted the original meaning.

concepts.label: Decknamen (Cover Names)
concepts.definition_long:
Decknamen (singular Deckname; from German, 'cover names') is a scholarly term for the encoded or pseudonymous names systematically used by alchemical writers to disguise the true identity of the materials, substances, and processes described in their texts. The term was introduced into the modern history of alchemy principally by William R. Newman, who discussed it in detail in his article 'Decknamen or Pseudochemical Language? Eirenaeus Philalethes and Carl Jung' (Revue d'Histoire des Sciences 49, 1996). Newman showed that alchemy's apparent obscurity often reflects a deliberate system of cover names rather than mystical allegory: substances like 'sericon,' 'green lion,' 'adrop,' 'red lion,' 'vitriol,' and 'venus' referred consistently (if not always uniformly) to identifiable chemical materials, and that unpacking these Decknamen makes it possible to reconstruct actual alchemical procedures from seemingly impenetrable texts.

Jennifer M. Rampling, in Osiris (2014), extends Newman's concept by showing that Decknamen were not static referents but were themselves subject to reinterpretation over time through the process of 'practical exegesis': the same term — such as sericon in the Ripley tradition — could shift from denoting red lead in a 15th-century manuscript to denoting antimony in a 17th-century printed edition, as successive readers glossed and adapted texts in light of their own practical experience and contemporary chemical fashions. The resulting 'uncoupling' of textual accounts from their original traditions means that the printed versions of alchemical texts most accessible to modern scholars may represent substantially reinterpreted versions of the original material. Decknamen are thus both an obstacle to historical interpretation (requiring unpacking before procedures can be identified) and an index of change in alchemical practice over time (since shifts in their meaning mark points where practitioners diverged from their sources). The scholarly method of decoding Decknamen through comparative analysis of manuscripts, laboratory reconstruction, and early modern lexicons (such as Martin Ruland's Lexicon Alchemiae, Frankfurt, 1612) has been central to the revival of serious laboratory-history approaches to alchemy since the 1980s.
